paragraphs.text: The sabbath in the Hebrew hath its name from resting ( שׁáú), and is near allied to two other words, the first whereof signifieth to sit still ( éשׁá), and the second to worship and give praise ( שׁáú). On this day they met for works of piety (as sacrificing, reading and expounding the Scriptures, praying, singing, as here, &c.) and of mercy, Mat 12:2-8; Mat 12:11-12. And this psalm, treating of God’s great works, was purposely set for a canon of sanctifying that day called by the Jews the queen of days; in praise whereof, before and after meat, they daily say certain verses.
paragraphs.anchor: A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day

paragraphs.text: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord] And the sabbath day is a good time to do it in; for then (as Kimchi here noteth) men are at leisure and liberty to do it most solemnly; the better day the better deed.

And to sing praises unto thy name] The psalmist commends it, and presently sets upon the doing of it. So Psa 122:6-7, he no sooner bids pray for the peace of Jerusalem, but himself prays, "Peace be within thy walls," &c.

Every morning, that God may have the firstfruits of the day, but especially on the sabbath morning, when we awake and rise, ad quietem et ad delicias animi et corporis, as Kimchi here hath it. The Jews bless God at the sabbath’s coming in and going out.
paragraphs.anchor: To show forth thy lovingkindness in the morning

paragraphs.text: Breaking our sleep for that purpose; yea, we must be in the fear of the Lord all the day long, Pro 23:17, how much more on the sabbath day! then our whole work must be ravished in spirit, doing no work, but such as whereby we either bless God or look to receive a blessing from God; none but such as wherein we would the Lord should find us at his coming; which Lactantius saith will be on the sabbath day.
paragraphs.anchor: And thy faithfulness in the night

paragraphs.text: This was part of the Jewish pedagogy; and teacheth us to use all lawful means to enforce ourselves to that, whereunto we are so dull and backward.
paragraphs.anchor: Upon an instrument of ten strings, &c.

paragraphs.text: And I will improve this cheerfulness to thankfulness, Jas 5:13. On the sabbath we ought solummodo spiritualibus gaudiis repleri, to be filled with spiritual joys only, saith the Council of Paris, held A.D. 820.
paragraphs.anchor: For thou, Lord, hast made me glad, &c.

paragraphs.text: sc. The works of creation, administration, but especially of redemption.
paragraphs.anchor: I will triumph in the works of thy hands

paragraphs.text: Surely so great that I cannot utter them, and must, therefore, thus vent myself by an exclamation.
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord, how great are thy works!

paragraphs.text: Expleri mentem nequeo, ardescoque tuendo
(Virgil.)
Here, then, we must do as those Romans did, who, when they found a lake the depth whereof was unknown, they dedicated it to Victory. Cry, O the depth! and there rest us.
paragraphs.anchor: And thy thoughts are very deep

paragraphs.text: A sottish sensualist, who hath his soul for salt only, to keep his body from putrefying (as we say of swine); he takes no knowledge of God’s great works, but grunts and goes his ways, contenting himself with a natural use of the creatures, as beasts do.
paragraphs.anchor: A brutish man knoweth not

paragraphs.text: This the fool admireth, calling the proud happy, &c., Mal 3:15, and not considering that that proud grass shall be mown down, and that that flourish shall soon perish.
paragraphs.anchor: When the wicked spring as the grass, &c.

paragraphs.text: Not grow again, as mown grass doth: Exoriuntur ut exurantur. It is but as Haman’s banquet before execution.
paragraphs.anchor: It is that they shall be destroyed for ever

paragraphs.text: q.d. Flourish the wicked never so much, shoot they up never so high, thou art higher, and in the thing wherein they deal proudly thou art above them, Exo 18:11.
paragraphs.anchor: But thou, Lord, art most high, &c.

paragraphs.text: A tree that groweth not in these cold climates, but where it doth is noted for tall, constantly green, long lived, sweet, firm, straight, &c., εμπεδοφυλλος (Theoph.).
paragraphs.anchor: The righteous shall flourish like the palm

paragraphs.text: Nititur in pondus palma et consurgit in altum;
Quo magis et premitur, hoc mage tollit onus.
Though it hath many weights at the top, and many snakes at the bottom, yet is still saith, Nec premor, nee perimor.
Not like grass, as the wicked do, Psa 92:7.
paragraphs.anchor: Like a cedar

paragraphs.text: Having taken deep root there. Hypocrites are only thrust in, as a stake, into the earth. Mnason was an old disciple, Andronicus and Junia were in Christ before Paul, and therefore of note among the apostles for well-rooted and fruited, Rom 16:7.
paragraphs.anchor: Those that be planted

paragraphs.text: In Christ, and under the ordinances.
paragraphs.anchor: In the courts of our God

paragraphs.text: Quantumvis veteres, non veterascent, though old, yet shall they retain their former vigour and verdure, and be like that Persian tree in Theophrastus, that at the same time doth bud, blossom, and bear fruit, pullulantes et succulentae.
paragraphs.anchor: They shall still bring forth fruit in old age

paragraphs.text: Vividi et vegeti (Bucholcer), not as the Brabanti or Flemings, qui quo magis senescunt, eo magis stultescunt, saith Erasmus, the elder the foolisher; nor as Trapezuntius, who outlived all his learning; but as Moses, whose sight failed not, his heat abated not; as wine, the older the better; as the sun, which shineth most amiably toward the descent.
paragraphs.anchor: They shall be fat and flourishing

paragraphs.text: This is one of their principal fruits, to give God a testimonial, such as good old Moses doth, Deu 32:4.
